**CHADDS FORD, Pa.** — Andrew Wyeth, one of the most prominent American realist painters of the 20th century, has died at his home in Pennsylvania. He was 91.

Wyeth gained widespread acclaim for his poignant, highly detailed depictions of rural American landscapes and figures, primarily capturing the people and surroundings of his hometown of Chadds Ford, Pennsylvania, and his summer home in Cushing, Maine. 

He was best known for his 1948 masterpiece, *Christina's World*, a haunting image of a young woman lying in a field, gazing up at a distant farmhouse. The painting became an enduring icon of American art history. Decades later, Wyeth drew national attention again with the unearthing of the "Helga" series—a collection of more than 200 secret, intimate portraits of his neighbor, Helga Testorf, created over a 15-year period without the knowledge of his wife or the public.

Throughout his long and prolific career, Wyeth received numerous high honors. In 2007, he was awarded the National Medal of Arts, the nation's highest honor for artists, presented by President George W. Bush.

Following the announcement of his passing, President Bush issued a statement remembering the painter for his deep impact on the country's cultural history, describing Wyeth as a visionary artist whose work captured the heart and spirit of the American landscape. 

Wyeth leaves behind a monumental legacy as a master of watercolor and egg tempera, whose work challenged abstract trends to remain fiercely grounded in traditional American realism.
